## 🔴 Open — follow-up sweep (2026-10-04)

Targeted at the four areas the 2026-09-30 sweep left **partial** (its own
"Notes on this sweep" named `server/app.py`, `logging_core/db_sink.py`, the
OpenAI Responses codec, and the middleware/lifespan). #345 is the
`server/app.py` result and is reproduced by executing code, not by reading it.

### 345. Realtime sessions are priced and logged but never charged to the key

**Severity:** 🔴 Critical · **Status: fixed** — round 135 (`tests/test_fix_round135.py`; fixed 2026-10-12)

**Files:** `wiwi/server/app.py:515-517` (`_bill_realtime_session`),
`wiwi/auth/service.py` (no such method)

`/v1/realtime` closes a session by calling `_bill_realtime_session`, which
prices the peak usage, settles the deployment's token counters, writes the
request-log row, and then charges the virtual key:

```python
if state.auth is not None:
    with contextlib.suppress(Exception):
        await state.auth.record_spend(info.key_id, priced, ctx)
```

**`AuthService` has no `record_spend` method.** The public surface is
`apply_spend_trueup`, `authenticate`, `count_keys`, `create_key`,
`delete_key`, `evict`, `expire_keys`, `get_key`, `key_owner`, `list_keys`,
`list_keys_for_owner`, `release_budget_reservation`, `reserve_budget`,
`set_disabled`, `startup`, `update_key`, `update_spend`. `record_spend` exists
only as the *nested closure* inside `run_chat_like` (`app.py:1490`) — it was
never a method, so `state.auth.record_spend` raises `AttributeError` on every
call, and the surrounding `contextlib.suppress(Exception)` swallows it with no
log, no counter and no /health field.

**Probe** (`realtime.enabled`, one virtual key with `max_budget=1.00`, a
10 000-in/10 000-out session on a model priced at 1e-4/1e-3):

```
state.auth.record_spend          -> '<<MISSING>>'
budget cap                      : $1.0
logged request cost for session : $11.000000
vkeys.spend_to_date after bill  : $0.000000
vkeys.max_budget                : $1.000000
spend_charge_failures counter   : 0
```

So an $11 session is priced, logged and visible in the admin console, and the
key is charged **$0.00**. Three consequences:

1. **A budget cap is a no-op on this surface.** `max_budget` is the one control
   a self-hosted gateway exists to offer; realtime is an unmetered hole in it.
   The key's `spend_to_date` never moves, so neither `over_budget`
   (`auth/service.py:114-121`) nor the 402 pre-flight refusal
   (`app.py:2777-2781`) ever fires for a realtime key.
2. **It is silent in the worst way.** Unlike AUDIT #179 and #324 — both of
   which make a failed charge loud with `spend_charge_failed` and a
   `spend_charge_failures` counter — this path cannot even be observed. The
   request log says the request cost $11 and the key says it spent nothing;
   nothing reconciles the two.
3. **The `suppress` is load-bearing for the bug, not for the design.** The
   intent of `with contextlib.suppress(Exception)` is "accounting must never
   500 a served turn" (the AUDIT #24 rule, honoured correctly in the nested
   `record_spend` at `app.py:1535-1557`). But it converts a *programming
   error* into a silent no-op, which is exactly the `ecc:silent-failure`
   class that AUDIT #332 already flags one function away. The sibling fix in
   round 112 is the model to follow: log, count, and retry through
   `apply_spend_trueup`.

**Fix sketch:** charge through the real API — `update_spend` with the same
release-first/charge-once shape as the nested `record_spend`, falling back to
`apply_spend_trueup` — or promote that closure to an `AuthService` method so
both call sites share one implementation (AGENTS.md rule 4: no second
convention beside an existing one). Replace the bare `suppress` with the
#179 guard rails: `spend_charge_failed` log + `spend_charge_failures` counter +
`apply_spend_trueup` retry. Realtime is also the only surface that skips the
admission-time `reserve_budget` (`app.py:1924-1950`), so it needs neither the
reservation nor its release.

**Test:** none exists — `tests/test_realtime.py` asserts the *peak-usage*
selection (`:244`) and the relay, never that a key is charged.

**Resolved in round 135** (`tests/test_fix_round135.py`). `_bill_realtime_session`
now charges via `state.auth.apply_spend_trueup(info.key_id, priced)` — the
unconditional true-up `record_spend` itself applies for an over-cap request
(the upstream really served these tokens, so the cap records them and only
blocks FUTURE requests) — and the bare `suppress` is replaced with the #179
guard rails: a `realtime_spend_charge_failed` log plus a
`spend_charge_failures` increment, so an unenforceable cap is visible in
/health and /metrics instead of vanishing. Realtime still skips the
admission-time `reserve_budget` (correct: it has no pre-flight estimate, and
its charge is a single unconditional true-up at close), so no reservation leak
is introduced. The regression test proves `spend_to_date` moves for a
budget-capped key and that a broken charge is counted, not silent.

### 346. A crash between reserve and settle leaks `budget_reserved` across restarts, permanently

**Severity:** 🟠 High · **Status: fixed** — re-verified 2026-10-13 (sweep).
`AuthService.startup` runs `UPDATE vkeys SET budget_reserved = 0` on every boot
(`wiwi/auth/service.py:270`): nothing is in flight at startup, so any non-zero
value is by definition an orphan. Body preserved unchanged.

**Files:** `wiwi/auth/service.py:657-681` (`release_budget_reservation`),
`:614-655` (`reserve_budget`), `:114-121` (`over_budget`),
`wiwi/server/app.py:1924-1956` (the reserve site)

Round 112 (#324) moved budget enforcement to admission: `reserve_budget`
adds `est/4·1e-6 + 1e-4` to a new `budget_reserved` column, and
`over_budget` reads `spend_to_date + budget_reserved >= max_budget` so
in-flight commitments block admission. The release is best-effort by design
(`app.py:1580`, `:2450`), which is correct — but a reservation whose
**process dies** between reserve and release is never reconciled. There is no
startup reset, no TTL, and no process-generation stamp: `budget_reserved` is
a plain persisted column, so the leaked amount outlives every restart and
permanently shrinks the key's usable headroom.

The release path's own docstring identifies the hazard and fixes only half of
it (`auth/service.py:663-666`): the `max(…, 0)` clamp stops a *negative*
balance from inflating headroom "from a crash-era stale reservation" — the
audit author saw the crash case and defended against the sign, not the
magnitude. A stale reservation is positive, and positive is exactly the
direction that disarms the cap.

**Probe** (key with `max_budget=0.01`; one request reserves its full estimate,
then the process is torn down without releasing):

```
reserve_budget(0.010) of a $0.01 cap -> True
AFTER RESTART
  spend_to_date   : $0.0
  budget_reserved : $0.01   <-- never billed, never refunded
  real headroom   : $0.0100
  usable headroom : $0.0000   <-- what admission actually sees
reserve_budget(0.0001) -> False   (a trivial request the key could easily afford)
  -> REFUSED: a key with real headroom cannot be served at all.
```

A key that has spent **nothing** and has its **full budget intact** is
permanently refused at admission after one unclean shutdown mid-request. There
is no admin affordance for it either — `/admin/keys/*` can raise `max_budget`
but nothing zeroes `budget_reserved`, and `list_keys` only *reports* it
(`auth/service.py:723`). The blast radius scales with how large a request was
in flight when the process died: the leaked amount is that request's estimate,
so a gateway serving long-context requests can strand a key on a single crash.

**Fix sketch:** treat the column as process-scoped, the way the round-112
journal-owner fix treats durability. Zero `budget_reserved` for every key in
`AuthService.startup` (nothing is in flight at startup, so any non-zero value
is by definition orphaned), or stamp reservations with the owning process
generation and expire them. Zeroing at startup is one idempotent UPDATE and
needs no schema change.

**Test:** none — `tests/test_fix_round112.py` covers reserve/refund within one
process lifetime, which is precisely the case that works.

### 347. The 402 budget refusal leaks the rate-limit slot it already reserved, and the leak is global

**Severity:** 🟠 High · **Status: fixed** — round 162 (`tests/test_fix_round162.py`)

The 402 path now refunds the reservation it took:
`await state.limiter.release(info.key_id, request_id)` before returning. The
release is identity-matched and removes the event from BOTH the key's and the
global window, so the cross-tenant leak is closed.

**Files:** `wiwi/server/app.py:1909` (`enforce_rate_limit`), `:1937-1949`
(the 402 return), `:1951-1956` (`ctx` construction, *after* the return)

`_chat_like` reserves a rate-limit slot **first** (`:1909`), then attempts the
budget reservation (`:1929`) and returns 402 when it is refused (`:1937-1949`) —
**without calling `_release_tpm_reservation`**. The `RequestContext` carrying
`budget_reserved` is not even constructed until `:1951`, so no enclosing
`finally` can reach the refund helper on this path. Every sibling early return
does call it (`:2069`, `:2121`, `:2154`, `:2182`, `:2273`, `:2282`); this one
was added by round 112 after that convention was written and was not converted.

The slot is unrecoverable: `RateLimiter.release` only removes events matching
that request id (`wiwi/ratelimit/memory.py:233`), and nothing else reclaims it
for the rest of the 60 s window.

**Probe** (`global_rpm=100`, one key with `max_budget=1e-9, rpm=2`):

```
req0: status=402 global:rpm=1 key:rpm=1  LEAK +1
req1: status=402 global:rpm=2 key:rpm=2  LEAK +1
req2: status=429 global:rpm=2 key:rpm=2
```

Two requests that never reached an upstream fully throttle the key. Worse, the
leaked event sits in the **global** scope, so it crosses tenants — with
`global_rpm=3`, three 402s from capped keys lock an unrelated uncapped key out:

```
capped req 0 -> 402
capped req 1 -> 402
capped req 2 -> 402
global:rpm events leaked by capped keys: 3
innocent key request -> 429          <-- unrelated, uncapped key, locked out
```

**Consequence:** availability. A single caller holding one budget-capped key
can throttle the whole gateway at any configured `global_rpm`/`global_tpm`,
one slot per refused request per window. This is the mirror image of AUDIT #285
(double-reserve), and its fix note claims "every early return between reserve and
settle funnels through here" — this return predates that claim.

**Fix sketch:** construct `ctx` above the reserve block so one `finally` owns
every post-reserve return, or call `await _release_tpm_reservation(info, refused)`
on the 402 path exactly as `:2069` does.

### 348. `lifespan` teardown is unguarded: one failing `stop()` skips every later one, including engine disposal

**Severity:** 🟠 High · **Status: fixed** — round 162 (`tests/test_fix_round162.py`)

Each worker's `stop()` now runs through a local `_stop(name, stop)` helper that
absorbs and logs a failure, and `state.shutdown()` (the engine disposal) runs
in its own guarded block. The order is unchanged — the DB-touching workers
still stop before the engine is disposed.

**Files:** `wiwi/server/app.py:1248-1266` (the whole teardown half),
`:1144-1152` (`AppState.shutdown` — `shutdown_event`, log pumps, engine dispose)

Twelve bare sequential `await X.stop()` calls with **no `try/finally`, no
`suppress`, no aggregation**. The first one to raise aborts every later stop
*and* `state.shutdown()` at `:1266`. Starlette's `Router.lifespan` does
`await receive()` inside the `async with` and re-raises, so **any exception
raised while serving** — including the `CancelledError` of a hard SIGINT —
skips the identical teardown half.

Every one of these workers is a third-party-or-local background task
(`tape_store.py:587`, `recovery.py:319`, `retention.py:48`, the three
`*_auto_refresh.py`, `response_store.py:139`) and none is individually guarded.
`retention.stop()` is the lone exception that suppresses internally
(`retention.py:54-55`) — the convention exists in the codebase and the lifespan
does not follow it.

**Probe** (a) — `journals.stop` (the *first* teardown await) raising:

```
B: lifespan exited with: journals.stop failed
[B: after] cline_refresh=RUNNING workbuddy_refresh=RUNNING opencode=RUNNING
           cline_version_refresh=RUNNING workbuddy_version_refresh=RUNNING
           retention=RUNNING journals=RUNNING
           shutdown_event_set=False dbpool=StaticPool
```

**Probe** (b) — no monkeypatch at all, just an exception inside the served body:

```
A: lifespan exited with: handler blew up
[A: after] ... journals=RUNNING sd_event_set=False
```

Control on the clean path is correct (`[after normal exit] ... sd_event=True`),
so the defect is the *sequencing*, not a missing or misordered stop: all nine
start/stop pairs match, and the DB-touching workers correctly stop before
`state.shutdown()` disposes the engine (`:1263`, `:1266`).

**Consequence:** `shutdown_event` is never set, so the `/admin/stream` SSE
keepalive loop (`app.py:3153-3157`, whose only break condition is `shutdown`)
never returns — the exact "hangs at *Waiting for connections to close*" the
comment says it exists to prevent. The engine is never disposed (`:1152`).
Seven orphaned tasks keep polling providers and holding sockets and DB
connections, and `tracer.shutdown()` (`:1254`) leaves the OTLP exporter
unflushed.

**Fix sketch:** `try: ... finally:` around the teardown half with
`await asyncio.gather(*stops, return_exceptions=True)` and a log per failure
(mirroring `retention.py:48-58`); `AsyncExitStack` also covers the
exception-during-serve case.

### 349. `/metrics` returns the SPA's `index.html` (HTTP 200) when Prometheus is disabled

**Severity:** 🟡 Medium · **Status: fixed** — round 162 (`tests/test_fix_round162.py`)

**Files:** `wiwi/server/app.py:2905` (route registered only inside
`if config.router_settings.prometheus_enabled:`), `:5844-5853`
(`SPAStaticFiles.get_response`), `:5860` (the catch-all mount)

**Fix (round 162).** The metrics route is now registered
**unconditionally**, and answers a truthful 404 with a plain-text
explanation when the exporter is off:

```python
@app.get(metrics_path)
async def prometheus_metrics(request: Request):
    if not config.router_settings.prometheus_enabled:
        return PlainTextResponse(
            "Prometheus metrics are disabled. Set "
            "router_settings.prometheus_enabled: true to enable this "
            "endpoint.\n",
            media_type="text/plain; charset=utf-8",
            status_code=404,
        )
```

The route used to be registered only inside
`if config.router_settings.prometheus_enabled:`, so with Prometheus off —
the DEFAULT — the path had no handler at all and the SPA catch-all
answered it with `index.html` and a 200. A scraper then recorded the
SPA's HTML as a successful scrape, and the operator's "is Prometheus up?"
check read green.

**Probe** (default config):

```
GET /metrics   -> 200 text/html; charset=utf-8
GET /metrics/  -> 200 text/html; charset=utf-8
```

**Probe** (after the fix, default config):

```
GET /metrics   -> 404 text/plain; charset=utf-8   ("Prometheus metrics are disabled...")
```

**Tests:** `test_metrics_path_is_not_the_spa_when_prometheus_is_disabled`,
`test_metrics_path_still_serves_metrics_when_enabled`.

**Consequence:** a scrape expecting `text/plain` gets 200 HTML. Prometheus's
`up` stays **1** while every metric is unparseable — a silent monitoring black
hole whose failure mode is precisely "looks healthy". Contrast `/health`,
`/public/models`, `/auth/me`, `/admin/*` and `/v1/*`, which all correctly return
JSON because they are registered above the mount.

**Fix sketch:** register the route unconditionally and return
`_err(404, "not_found_error", "metrics disabled", …)` from the body when the
setting is off, rather than not registering it at all.

### 350. `previous_response_id` drops the entire user-side conversation history

**Severity:** 🔴 Critical · **Status: fixed** — round 162 (`tests/test_fix_round162.py`) — re-tested 2026-10-13 (sweep).

The fix reads BOTH halves of the stored turn: `with_history` now takes the
previous turn's `input_items` as well as its `output`, and the input half is
prepended FIRST (the conversation order is user-then-assistant). The store
already recorded both halves — `StoredResponse.input_items` was written by two
call sites and read by none.
Code read of the live path: `_chat_like` loads the stored transcript before the
codec and 404s on a store miss (`wiwi/server/app.py:1959-1976`), and
`with_history` prepends the items / wraps a string input as a user message
(`wiwi/wire/openai_responses.py:249-264`) — the "drops the entire history"
shape is no longer reachable through the app. The register entry needs an
end-to-end replay probe (two chained `previous_response_id` turns through a
temporary app + ResponseStore) before it can be closed as fixed; until that
runs, the status is not being flipped.

**Files:** `wiwi/server/app.py:1867` (`codec_history(body, prev.output.get("output", []))`),
`wiwi/wire/openai_responses.py:239-255` (`with_history`),
`wiwi/server/response_store.py:51` (`StoredResponse.input_items`)

The store records **both** halves of a turn — `put(..., input_items, output)`
at `app.py:2260` and `:2430`, persisted in the `input_json` column and read
back at `response_store.py:98`. But `with_history` is handed **only**
`prev.output["output"]`. `StoredResponse.input_items` is written by two call
sites and read by **none** — `prev.input_items` appears nowhere in the repo
(grep-verified). So the previous turn's *user* message never reaches the
upstream.

**Probe** (three chained `/v1/responses` turns against a mocked Anthropic
upstream, capturing the upstream body each turn):

```
turn2 upstream: [{"role":"user","content":"Q2-SECOND"}]   + assistant A1
turn3 upstream: [{"role":"user","content":"Q3-THIRD"}]    + assistant A2
>>> Q1 present on turn 3: False
>>> Q2 present on turn 3: False
```

The model sees `[assistant A1, user Q2]` on turn 2 and never learns what the
user originally asked. Stateless callers that resend `input` in full are
unaffected, so this bites exactly the stateful `previous_response_id` path —
the documented spec-B feature. `AUDIT.md:7648` claims the store keeps "the
request's normalized input items so the next turn can be rebuilt"; that half
is never read.

**Consequence:** every stateful multi-turn Responses/Codex session silently
loses context and appears to forget what it was asked, with no error anywhere.

**Fix sketch:** read `prev.input_items` at `app.py:1867` and prepend it inside
`with_history` ahead of `previous_output`, so `decode_request`'s existing
`previous_output` path carries both halves.

### 351. A non-string `reasoning.effort` 500s every non-OpenAI deployment (the inbound half of #288)

**Severity:** 🔴 Critical · **Status: fixed** — re-verified 2026-10-11 (round 127 sweep). `effort_to_thinking_budget` now guards with `isinstance(effort, str)` (`wiwi/ir/types.py`) and the Responses decoder coerces via `_effort_str` (`wiwi/wire/openai_responses.py`): `reasoning.effort` of `["low"]`/`{"a":1}`/`5` decodes to `reasoning_effort=None`, so nothing unhashable reaches an adapter. Body preserved unchanged.


**Severity:** 🔴 Critical · **Status: open**

**Files:** `wiwi/wire/openai_responses.py:411-413` (effort read untyped),
`wiwi/ir/types.py:296` (`_EFFORT_BUDGETS.get(effort)`),
reached from `wiwi/providers/anthropic_adapter.py:520` and
`wiwi/providers/gemini_adapter.py:190`

The Responses decoder forwards any client value into
`GenParams.reasoning_effort` (typed `str | None`) with no coercion. A list or
dict effort is unhashable, so the `.get` in `effort_to_thinking_budget` raises
`TypeError` inside the adapter's encode path.

**Probe** (direct — no HTTP layer needed, so this is unambiguous):

```
GenParams.reasoning_effort = ['low']
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "wiwi/providers/anthropic_adapter.py", line 520, in encode_request
    budget = g.effective_thinking_budget()
  File "wiwi/ir/types.py", line 264, in effective_thinking_budget
    return effort_to_thinking_budget(self.reasoning_effort)
  File "wiwi/ir/types.py", line 296, in effort_to_thinking_budget
    return _EFFORT_BUDGETS.get(effort)
TypeError: cannot use 'list' as a dict key (unhashable type: 'list')
```

Through the full stack this is an HTTP 500 `internal gateway error` before any
upstream call, on **every** Anthropic and Gemini deployment. AUDIT #288 fixed
this exact crash on the *outbound* openai/openrouter adapters
(`tests/test_fix_round96.py`) but the **inbound** Responses decoder — the only
place a client-supplied effort enters — was never guarded. Same class as #327.
`openai_chat.py`'s `reasoning_effort` is untyped in the same way, so the class
is not closed by fixing one codec.

**Fix sketch:** guard in `effort_to_thinking_budget` with
`isinstance(effort, str)` — that closes the class for every present and future
caller — and coerce at the two inbound decoders.

### 352. A non-list/non-string `input` is silently discarded; the gateway answers 200 with an empty prompt

**Severity:** 🟠 High · **Status: fixed** — re-verified 2026-10-13 (sweep).
The missing guard now exists: `orp.decode_request({"model": "m", "input": {…}/123/true})`
all raise ``DialectError("'input' must be a string or a list")", matching both
siblings (executed probe, `openai_responses.py`). Body preserved unchanged.

**Files:** `wiwi/wire/openai_responses.py:270-277` (`else: items = []`),
`wiwi/server/app.py:1740-1752` (`_stored_input_items` → `[]`)

The two sibling codecs both reject the equivalent shape:
`openai_chat.py:77-83` and `anthropic_messages.py:53-57` raise
`DialectError("'messages' must be a list")`. The Responses codec is the only
one with no guard, so `input: {...}`, `input: 123` or `input: true` produces
`items = []`.

**Probe:**

```
input=dict (OpenAI 400s this shape) -> HTTP 200   upstream messages=[]
input=123                            -> HTTP 200   upstream messages=[]
input=true                           -> HTTP 200   upstream messages=[]
control: input="hi"                  -> HTTP 200   upstream messages=[{'role':'user','content':'hi'}]
control: chat messages=123           -> HTTP 400   "'messages' must be a list"
```

The user's entire prompt is dropped, the upstream is called with
`messages: []`, it returns 200, and tokens are billed for a model answering a
question nobody asked. The same shape also zeroes the stored transcript, so the
next `previous_response_id` turn compounds #350.

**Fix sketch:** raise `DialectError("'input' must be a string or a list")`,
mirroring both siblings.

### 353. `audit_logs` has no retention, no cap and no rollup

**Severity:** 🟠 High · **Status: fixed** — round 162 (`tests/test_fix_round162.py`)

`db_sink` gained `prune_old_audit(retention_days)`,
`enforce_audit_cap(max_rows)` and `audit_log_count()`; the retention sweep now
runs both prunes against `audit_logs`. The cap drops the OLDEST rows, keeping
the newest, with the same `(ts DESC, id DESC)` boundary shape as the request
log's cap.

**Files:** `wiwi/logging_core/db_sink.py:1198-1206` (`write_audit`, INSERT
only), `:774` (`idx_audit_logs_ts`), vs `wiwi/logging_core/retention.py:96-97`
(`sweep()` touches only `request_logs`)

`grep "DELETE" db_sink.py` returns exactly one statement —
`DELETE FROM request_logs` (`:682`). No `DELETE FROM audit_logs` exists
anywhere in the codebase, and `LogRetention.sweep()` calls only
`prune_old_requests` and `enforce_log_cap`.

**Consequence, two defects in one:**

1. **Unbounded growth.** Every admin key/deploy/provider/pricing mutation is a
   permanent row. `log_retention_days` and `log_max_rows` are silently
   non-applicable to this table, on any gateway an operator actually
   administers.
2. **Read amplification.** `read_audit` orders by `ts DESC, id DESC` but the
   only index is `idx_audit_logs_ts(ts)`. The `id DESC` tiebreak forces a sort
   of every matching row, and `/admin/logs/audit?limit=5000` (`app.py:4671`)
   is polled by the console — so this degrades into a scan per refresh.

**Fix sketch:** add `audit_logs` to `LogRetention.sweep()` (age prune or row
cap) and add `CREATE INDEX ... ON audit_logs(ts, id)`.

---

### 354. `rollup_and_prune` has no cross-process lock — concurrent sweeps double-count the table

**Severity:** 🟠 High · **Status: fixed** — round 162 (`tests/test_fix_round162.py`)

The sweep now runs under a DATABASE-level lock — a row in a new `sweep_locks`
table, taken with a conditional insert so exactly one process wins. A row is
used rather than a Postgres advisory lock because the gateway also runs on
SQLite (no advisory lock) and because a row can carry an age: a process that
died holding the lock leaves a stale row, reclaimed by its TTL.

**Files:** `wiwi/logging_core/db_sink.py:567-687` (the whole transaction),
`:660-663` (`if not groups: return 0` inside it),
`wiwi/logging_core/retention.py:96-97`

Each sweep accumulates rollup groups from a snapshot with no lock, then does an
**additive** `ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE SET requests = request_rollups.requests
+ excluded.requests`. That form is correct for *sequential* repeated sweeps and
wrong for concurrent ones: under READ COMMITTED, sweep B's upsert can commit
before sweep A's delete, so A's delete removes rows B already counted.

**Probe** (30 rows, two overlapping `prune_old_requests` calls):

```
returns: [30, 0]
rollup SUM(requests): 60   raw rows left: 0
single-run control: rollup SUM(requests) = 30
```

30 requests in, **60** reported. Reachable with two uvicorn workers against one
Postgres, or two gateway instances against one DB. Rollups are never pruned, so
the inflation is permanent, and it hits cost and spend on the dashboard.
`_existing_histograms` merging repairs only `p95_hist`, not the additive
counters.

**Fix sketch:** take a Postgres advisory lock (`pg_try_advisory_xact_lock`) or a
row lock on a singleton row at the top of the transaction.

---

### 355. A Responses `reasoning` item replays with no `encrypted_content`

**Severity:** 🟠 High · **Status: fixed** — round 162 (`tests/test_fix_round162.py`)

The blob now has a carrier end to end: `ir.ThinkingPart.encrypted_content` and
`dl.ThinkingDelta.encrypted_content` (Codex streams its turns, so the
streaming path needs it too). The Responses decoder reads it, `_reasoning_item`
re-emits it, and the Responses-shaped outbound adapter both decodes and
re-encodes it. The field is omitted when absent, so an item with no blob does
not grow a fake one.

**Files:** `wiwi/wire/openai_responses.py:377-387` (the `reasoning` decode
arm), `:459-462` (`_reasoning_item`), `wiwi/ir/types.py:115` (`ThinkingPart`
has no blob field), `RESEARCH.md:26` and `:67`

Codex sends `include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"]` on **every** request and
must replay every output item verbatim including that blob (`RESEARCH.md:26`,
`:67`). `RESEARCH.md:107` names this exact hazard. The decoder reads only
`summary` and builds `ir.ThinkingPart(text=…, signature=None, data=None)` — the
blob has nowhere to live in the IR — and `_reasoning_item` never re-emits it.

**Probe:**

```
decoded reasoning part: ThinkingPart(text='plan', signature=None, data=None)
encrypted_content survived: False
-> anthropic upstream gets {"type":"thinking","thinking":"secret plan"}   # no signature
```

**Consequence:** the next turn sends reasoning history with the opaque blob
missing, which the Responses API rejects (`'encrypted_content' is required`),
so reasoning-model multi-turn through `/v1/responses` breaks on turn 2. Downstream
the blob degrades to plain text — an Anthropic upstream receives an unsigned
`thinking` block, which 400s for the same reason.

**Fix sketch:** add `encrypted_content: str | None` to `ir.ThinkingPart`,
decode it, re-emit it from `_reasoning_item`, and have `anthropic_adapter` skip
(or refuse) a `ThinkingPart` with no signature rather than send it unsigned.

---

### 356. A tool item's `item_id` uses the IR stream index, so streamed and sync ids disagree

**Severity:** 🟡 Medium · **Status: fixed** — round 162 (`tests/test_fix_round162.py`)

The tool item id now keys on the OUTPUT INDEX in all three places that mint
it (`ToolCallOpen`, the args-delta frame, and `_close_tool`), matching the
non-streaming `encode_response`, which already used the shared item counter.

**Files:** `wiwi/wire/openai_responses.py:761` (`ToolCallOpen` mints
`fc_{req_id}_{n}` from `d.index`), `:625` (`_close_tool` likewise), `:551-556`
(`encode_response` mints from a *different* counter)

`output_index` is bumped for **every** item (message, reasoning, tool);
`d.index` is the IR tool index. So with a message at `output_index` 0 and one
tool call, the stream mints `fc_<req>_0` at `output_index: 1`, while
`encode_response` for the same turn mints `fc_<req>_1` (it counts the message
first).

**Probe:**

```
stream: output_item.added oi=0 id=fc_r1_7    (d.index=7, output_index=0)
sync:   function_call fc_r1_3
-> same turn, two different ids for the same call
```

With non-monotonic IR indices the id sequence also runs *against*
`output_index`. A client that stores the streamed id and later references it
against the sync-shaped payload points at a different item.

**Fix sketch:** key both on `t["output_index"]` (or one dedicated monotonic item
counter) and reuse it from `encode_response`.

### 357. `ToolCallClose` in an order other than open order misorders `response.completed.output`

**Severity:** 🟡 Medium · **Status: fixed** — round 162 (`tests/test_fix_round162.py`)

`_item_done` now inserts the item at its `output_index` instead of appending
it, so the terminal `output[]` array is in the same order as the per-item
events. The contract permits batch closes in ANY order, so the close order
cannot be the display order.

**Files:** `wiwi/wire/openai_responses.py:604-609` (`_item_done` appends in
**close** order), `:829-832` (`_completed` sorts `sorted(self._tools)`)

`streaming/deltas.py` explicitly permits batch closes in any order ("Adapters
may hold several indices open at once and close them in a batch"). `self._output`
is built in close order, so the terminal payload's `output[]` disagrees with
`output_index`.

**Probe:**

```
--- parallel tools, Close(1) then Close(0)
   output_item.added oi=0 id=fc_req1_0
   output_item.added oi=1 id=fc_req1_1
   response.completed output_order_ids=['fc_req1_1', 'fc_req1_0']
```

**Consequence:** a client rebuilding the assistant turn from
`response.completed.response.output` rather than the per-item `done` events gets
tool calls in the wrong sequence relative to the text they bracket.

**Fix sketch:** insert at `idx` in `_item_done` rather than appending.

---

### 358. `stop_reason: context_window_exceeded` reports `status: "completed"`

**Severity:** 🟡 Medium · **Status: fixed** — round 162 (`tests/test_fix_round162.py`)

`_INCOMPLETE_REASONS` now also covers `context_window_exceeded` (mapped to the
spec's `max_output_tokens`, the closest existing value for a turn that did not
finish) and `pause_turn`. Both are stop reasons the IR carries precisely so
the client can react; reporting `status: "completed"` removed that signal.

**Files:** `wiwi/wire/openai_responses.py:428` (`_INCOMPLETE_REASONS`),
`:445-450` (`_response_obj`), `:823-825` (the `incomplete` test)

`_INCOMPLETE_REASONS` covers only `{"length", "content_filter"}`. An Anthropic
upstream returning `stop_reason: "model_context_window_exceeded"` is carried
verbatim as `context_window_exceeded` (`ir/translation.py:41`), and
`ir/types.py:17-24` documents that value as one of the three "stop" cannot
express. The client gets `status: "completed"` with no `incomplete_details`, so
it has no signal to trigger auto-compact — the exact failure the IR field
exists to prevent, and the exact symptom #272 recorded and closed as
"non-actionable". `compaction` and `pause_turn` behave the same way.

**Fix sketch:** map `context_window_exceeded` → `incomplete` /
`max_output_tokens` (the spec's own value) and `pause_turn` → `incomplete` with a
dedicated reason, in both `_INCOMPLETE_REASONS` and the `:823` test.

### 359. `json_schema.schema` is accepted unvalidated in all three codecs

**Severity:** ⚪ Low · **Status: fixed — round 174** (`tests/test_fix_round174.py`; wider than registered: the Chat codec's *inner* `schema` was unguarded too — `openai_chat.py:307` guarded only the wrapper — and a junk `name` rode along in all three. All three decoders now coerce a non-dict schema to `{"type":"object"}` and a non-string `name` to `None`; Chat keeps `json_object`'s schema `None` so no `json_schema` member leaks into that wire shape)

**Files:** `wiwi/wire/openai_responses.py:230-232`,
`wiwi/wire/openai_chat.py:305`, `wiwi/wire/anthropic_messages.py:392`

`{"text":{"format":{"type":"json_schema","name":"n","schema":"oops"}}}` puts the
string `"oops"` into `ResponseFormat.json_schema` (typed `dict | None`), which
`openai_adapter.py:301-304` forwards upstream as `"schema": "oops"`. The
upstream 400s naming nothing the caller sent — the class of AUDIT #186/#187.
No crash, hence low. `openai_chat.py:307` guards the same field; these two do not.

**Fix sketch:** `json_schema=(fmt.get("schema") if isinstance(..., dict) else
{"type":"object"})` in all three, matching the one that already does.

### 428. The request log never stored the error message the caller received

**Severity:** 🟠 Medium · **Status: fixed** (round 137)

**Files:** `wiwi/logging_core/events.py` (`LogEvent`),
`wiwi/core/gateway.py:build_log_event`, `wiwi/logging_core/db_sink.py`,
`web/src/pages/RequestLogs.tsx`

A failed request logs only `error_code` — the coarse `etype`
(`rate_limit_error`, `api_error`). The exact upstream message the caller
actually saw (`"openai-main rate limited: You exceeded your current quota…"`,
`"stream died: reset by peer"`) lived on `ctx.error.message` and was discarded
by `build_log_event`, so `/console/request-logs` could never reproduce a
failure's cause. Operators had to chase the same error through the provider's
own console, and a per-key vs. per-deployment attribution was impossible from
the log alone.

**Fix:** added `LogEvent.error_message`, populated in `build_log_event` from
`ctx.error.message` via the existing `_scrub_credentials` (a 401 upstream
quotes the rejected key verbatim, and the request log is shown to every admin
and mirrored into backups), persisted to a new `request_logs.error_message`
column (DDL + `_COLS` + `_row` + the `_migrate` ALTER list), and rendered in
the detail drawer below "Error code". Regression: `tests/test_fix_round137.py`.

### 429. The console `Drawer` portals to `<body>`, escaping the `[data-admin]` CSS-var scope — its panel background resolves to nothing and renders fully transparent

**Severity:** 🟠 Medium · **Status: fixed** — `overlayHost()` in
`web/src/components/ui.tsx` now portals both `Dialog` and `Drawer` into
`document.querySelector("[data-admin]")` (falling back to `document.body`).
Verified in a live browser at 375px and 1440px: the drawer panel computes
`rgb(14, 14, 14)` and the dialog `rgb(14, 14, 14)`, and neither layer
interleaves with the page behind it any more.

**Files:** `web/src/components/ui.tsx:777-794` (`Drawer`, the
`createPortal(..., document.body)`), `web/src/styles.css:209-213` (the
`[data-admin]` block that defines `--admin-surface-elevated`)

Every admin design-token variable is declared inside the `[data-admin]`
selector, so they only resolve for descendants of that element. `Drawer`
portals its panel to `document.body`, which is **not** inside `[data-admin]`,
so the panel's `bg-[var(--admin-surface-elevated)]` resolves to an undefined
value. The `background-color` computes to `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)`: the drawer has
no background at all. Verified in a live browser — the scrim's `bg-black/60`
also fails to resolve, so the request-logs table shows straight through the
drawer and the two layers' text interleaves and is unreadable. Reproduces at
both 1280px and 375px, on every drawer in the console.

`Dialog` (`ui.tsx:681`) portals the same way but hardcodes `bg-black/70`, so
its scrim happens to survive — only the `Drawer` panel depends on a token.
Its panel does not: `bg-[var(--admin-surface-elevated)]` on the dialog panel
was equally undefined, so it was fixed by the same change.

**Fix:** either portal into the `[data-admin]` element instead of `document.body`
(keeps one source of truth for the tokens), or hoist the token block to
`:root`/`.dark` on `<html>` — which `main.tsx` already sets — and drop the
`[data-admin]` scoping. The second is the smaller change but widens every
token to the public marketing pages, so check for collisions first.

**Fixed** by taking the first option. The helper is shared by both overlays so
there is one convention, not a second beside the existing one.

## ✅ Fixed — multi-account Hermes + realtime follow-up (2026-10-13)

Found by reading back round 136 (`/admin/hermes/oauth/*` end to end, the Hermes
credential encode/decode path, the `hermes_auto_refresh` sweeper) and the
`/v1/realtime` WS surface against how every other Hermes deployment is shaped.
The round-136 per-account model is correct at the adapter and sweeper layer, but
the endpoints that *write* pool keys (label derivation, placeholder key,
in-place rotation, whole-pool disconnect), the console that reads `/status`,
and the realtime admission/billing path each still carry the pre-136 or
pre-existing assumptions. Entries #430-#442.

**Resolution (2026-10-14):** all thirteen entries are fixed and each carries an
inline `**Status: fixed**` line naming its round test file — #430/#431/#432/#433/
#434/#436/#441 in `tests/test_fix_round138.py`, #437/#439/#440 in
`tests/test_fix_round139.py`, #438 in `tests/test_fix_round140.py`, #442 in
`tests/test_fix_round141.py`. #435 is a console-only (TypeScript) fix with no
Python regression test. Full gate green at the time of writing: 3218 passed,
11 skipped, ruff clean.

### 430. The Hermes credential blob is stored as the pool-key label — plaintext `access_token` + `refresh_token` in the DB, the API, and every log row

**Severity:** 🔴 Critical · **Status: fixed** — round 138 (`tests/test_fix_round138.py::test_poll_label_is_the_account_label_not_the_credential_blob`; fixed 2026-10-14)

`/poll` now hands `_hermes_account_label(access)` to
`_unique_hermes_key_label` as the `base`, so the
`ProviderKey.label` is the account label and the
`hermes:{"access_token":…}` blob never reaches the label
column, `/status`, the key listing, or
`LogEvent.provider_key_label`. The regression asserts the label is
the email, not the blob.

**Files:** `wiwi/server/app.py:6081-6084` (`_unique_hermes_key_label(state,
provider, secret)`), `wiwi/server/app.py:6129` (`/status`), `wiwi/server/app.py:3409`
(generic key listing), `wiwi/logging_core/events.py:22`
(`LogEvent.provider_key_label`), `wiwi/providers/hermes_auto_refresh.py:248`
(`log.info("hermes_auto_refreshed", ...)`)

`/poll` computes the account's human label on the line above
(`_hermes_account_label(access)`, `:6083`) and passes it only into
`encode_credential`, then hands the *encoded secret blob itself* to the labeler
as its `base`. `_unique_hermes_key_label` treats `base` as a label string and
returns it verbatim when no collision exists, so the resulting
`ProviderKey.label` is the whole `hermes:{"access_token":…,"refresh_token":…}`
JSON.

Unlike `secret`, the label is **not** masked. `mask_key(k.secret)` guards the
secret in the key listing at `:3410`, but `:3409` returns `k.label`
unmasked; `/status` returns it at `:6129`; and `LogEvent.provider_key_label`
(`events.py:22`) carries it onto every request-log row this account serves,
which is rendered in `/console/request-logs` and included in
`GET /admin/backup`. The refresh sweeper's own log line
(`hermes_auto_refresh.py:248`) prints it too. So a long-lived access token and
a single-use refresh token sit in cleartext in the `provider_keys.label` column,
in the request log, and in the proxy log.

The exposure is also *permanent*: `_update_secret`
(`hermes_auto_refresh.py:251-269`) rewrites `k.secret` only, so the label keeps
the original (now dead) tokens after every rotation — the DB never ages it out.

**Fix sketch:** pass `_hermes_account_label(access)` as the labeler's `base`,
not `secret`.

### 431. The `hermes:pending` bootstrap key is created and never removed — it burns a guaranteed-401 request every rotation cycle

**Severity:** 🔴 Critical · **Status: fixed** — round 138 (`tests/test_fix_round138.py`; fixed 2026-10-14)

The bootstrap account is created with an empty key list and `/poll`
adds the first real key, so `hermes:pending` is never minted.
`/disconnect` also drops a lone placeholder by label rather than by
successful decode, so a leftover one is still removable.
`test_placeholder_helper_does_not_scatter_the_literal` pins the
sentinel to a single helper.

**Files:** `wiwi/server/app.py:5965-5979` (bootstrap `ProviderKey`), `wiwi/server/app.py:6089`
(`/poll` append), `wiwi/providers/hermes_oauth.py:276` (`credential_bearer`),
`wiwi/router/router.py:35-37` (`ProviderKey` defaults), `wiwi/server/app.py:6246`
(`/disconnect` filter)

Device-code login bootstraps a fresh provider account with
`ProviderKey(label="default", secret="hermes:pending")`, under a comment
claiming "`/poll` replaces that secret with the real `hermes:<token>` on
approval." `/poll` does not replace anything — it only **appends** a new
`ProviderKey` (`:6089`), so the placeholder survives the entire connect flow.

The placeholder is not inert. `decode_credential("hermes:pending")` returns
`None` (the body after the `hermes:` prefix is not JSON), so
`credential_bearer` falls through to its bare-prefix branch and returns the
literal string `pending` as the bearer. `ProviderKey` defaults to
`enabled=True, status="active"` (`router/router.py:35-37`), so the key sits in
smooth-WRR rotation alongside every real account and sends
`Authorization: Bearer pending` upstream on a share of all traffic — a
guaranteed 401 that trips the auto-refresh hook, which then cannot possibly
succeed for a key with no refresh token. `/disconnect` does not remove it
either: `:6246` only drops keys whose `decode_credential` succeeds, and this
one decodes to `None`.

**Fix sketch:** in `/poll`, drop the placeholder before appending — remove it
from `acct.keys` in memory **and** `await state.config_store.delete_key(
provider, "default")` — or have the bootstrap create the account with an empty
key list and let `/poll` add the first key.

### 432. `/refresh`'s `except AttributeError` fallback calls `_update_secret` on the `None` it just proved — consumes the single-use grant, then 500s

**Severity:** 🟠 High · **Status: fixed** — round 138 (`tests/test_fix_round138.py`; fixed 2026-10-14)

The `except AttributeError:` fallback is gone; the handler branches
explicitly on `state.hermes_refresh is None`. With no lifespan
worker, the threaded exchange writes the new secret to the pool key
directly and returns a relogin-required body instead of 500ing.

**Files:** `wiwi/server/app.py:6180-6212` (the fallback block), `wiwi/server/app.py:890`
(`state.hermes_refresh` initialized `None`), `wiwi/providers/hermes_oauth.py`
(`refresh_access_token`)

The intent of `except AttributeError:` at `:6181` is to catch
`state.hermes_refresh is None` (the attribute is initialized to `None` at
`:890`), and fall back to a direct threaded exchange. The fallback body then
does two things that defeat it: `:6193` calls
`state.hermes_refresh._update_secret(...)` on the object it just established is
`None`, and `:6208` reads `state.hermes_refresh._circuit` unconditionally.

Order matters and it is the wrong order. The threaded exchange at `:6186` runs
**first** and succeeds, rotating Nous's single-use refresh token server-side;
only then does `:6193` raise `AttributeError` on `None` — uncaught, because it
is raised inside an `except` handler. The endpoint 500s. The freshly minted
access token is discarded, the pool key still holds the now-consumed grant, and
the next refresh attempt gets `invalid_grant` → circuit dead → a human re-login,
triggered by one admin click.

Two secondary problems with the same lines: the fallback also masks genuine
`AttributeError`s raised *inside* `_refresh_locked` after a grant was consumed
(they take the same branch and 500 at the same place), and `:6208`'s
`state.hermes_refresh._circuit` is reached on the normal path too, so any
non-`AttributeError` failure from the worker leaves the same latent `None`
dereference.

**Fix sketch:** branch explicitly — `if state.hermes_refresh is None:` → inline
the exchange *and write the new secret directly to the pool key*; `else:` → call
`refresh_key_now(...)` — instead of catching `AttributeError`.

### 433. Whole-pool Hermes disconnect is memory-only — every account comes back after a restart

**Severity:** 🟠 High · **Status: fixed** — round 138 (`tests/test_fix_round138.py::test_whole_pool_disconnect_persists`; fixed 2026-10-14)

Labels removed in memory are collected and each one is passed to
`config_store.delete_key` unconditionally, so the whole-pool path is
as durable as the single-account one.

**Files:** `wiwi/server/app.py:6252-6254`, `wiwi/server/config_store.py:647-680`
(`ConfigStore.load_all`)

`/disconnect` filters `acct.keys` in memory and then calls
`config_store.delete_key` only `if label:`. The whole-pool disconnect — the
path an operator uses to remove *every* Nous account at once, i.e. the one that
should be unambiguous — therefore persists nothing. It clears the legacy
settings record and reports `disconnected: <count>`, so the UI shows the pool as
empty and the admin believes the tokens are gone.

They are not. `ConfigStore.load_all()` reloads every `provider_keys` row for
the account at startup and re-injects them into the router, so the accounts (and
their plaintext credential blobs) reappear on the next process start. The
single-account path does delete its row, so the two paths disagree about whether
disconnect is durable.

**Fix sketch:** collect the labels actually removed in the loop and
`await state.config_store.delete_key(provider, lbl)` for each, unconditionally.

### 434. Re-login appends a duplicate Hermes key instead of rotating that account in place — the stale copy then kills the account's circuit

**Severity:** 🟠 High · **Status: fixed** — round 138 (`tests/test_fix_round138.py::test_relogin_rotates_the_same_account_in_place`; fixed 2026-10-14)

`/poll` scans `acct.keys` for a key whose decoded credential label
matches the incoming account and overwrites that key's secret and DB
row instead of appending.

**Files:** `wiwi/server/app.py:5939-5953` (`_unique_hermes_key_label`),
`wiwi/server/app.py:6084-6089` (`/poll` label + append)

`_unique_hermes_key_label`'s docstring promises: "a second connect for the SAME
account reuses its existing label (so a re-login rotates that account in
place)." Neither half holds. `/poll` unconditionally appends a new
`ProviderKey` (`:6089`) rather than overwriting, and — see #430 — the dedup
`base` was the credential blob, so the base differs on every connect (a new
access token each time) and the "already taken" branch could never match even in
principle. Every connect, including a re-login of one account, silently
duplicates it.

The duplicate is not a harmless extra row. The stale key keeps the *previous*
single-use refresh grant, which the new login has already consumed. The sweeper
eventually presents it, Nous answers `invalid_grant`, and the account's circuit
is marked permanently dead — the AUDIT #169 failure mode, reintroduced through
a path that only appears on the second connect.

**Fix sketch:** before appending, scan `acct.keys` for a key whose
`decode_credential(k.secret).get("label")` equals the new account's label; if
found, overwrite that key's secret (and DB row) instead of appending.

### 435. The admin console was never updated for the multi-account Hermes `/status` — the Refresh button is permanently disabled

**Severity:** 🟠 High · **Status: fixed** (no Python test — console-only; fixed 2026-10-14)

`HermesStatusResponse` now declares the `accounts` array
(`web/src/api/types.ts`), and the new
`web/src/components/HermesAccounts.tsx` renders one row per account
(label, expiry, managed badge, per-row Refresh/Disconnect) with the
whole-pool action kept separate. `web/src/pages/HermesOAuth.tsx` and
`web/src/pages/ProviderDetail.tsx` both mount it via the `@/` alias.
`key_label` now threads through `hermesRefresh`/`hermesDisconnect`
(`web/src/api/client.ts`), and `disconnected` is a count. **There is
no Python regression test for this one** — it is a TypeScript-only
change and is verified by `tsc -b` + eslint at build time, not by
pytest.

**Files:** `web/src/api/types.ts:327-332` (`HermesStatusResponse`),
`web/src/pages/HermesOAuth.tsx:314,350,379`, `web/src/pages/ProviderDetail.tsx:1398-1418`,
`web/src/api/client.ts:484-492` (`hermesRefresh`/`hermesDisconnect`)

`HermesStatusResponse` still declares the pre-round-136 flat shape
`{connected, expires_at, needs_refresh, has_refresh_token}`, but the endpoint
returns `{connected, accounts: [{key_label, label, expires_at, managed, …}]}`
(`app.py:6107-6140`, AUDIT #427). TypeScript does not catch it — the extra
property is simply absent from the declared type, so `statusQ.data.expires_at`
reads `undefined` at runtime and the code compiles clean.

Consequences, all user-visible on the Hermes provider page: the "expires soon"
badge never appears, "Token expires" is always blank, and — because the button's
`disabled` predicate is `!statusQ.data?.has_refresh_token`
(`HermesOAuth.tsx:379`) and that field no longer exists — **the Refresh button
is permanently disabled**. That button is the operator's documented escape hatch
for a dead grant (`hermes_auto_refresh.py:157-159`), so the one control that
recovers a wedged account is unreachable from the console.

`hermesRefresh`/`hermesDisconnect` (`client.ts:484-492`) also send only
`{provider}`, so single-account targeting (`key_label`) is impossible from the
UI, and `disconnected` changed from a `boolean` to a count while the declared
response type still says `boolean`.

**Fix sketch:** update `HermesStatusResponse` to the `accounts` array, render one
row per account (label, expiry, managed badge, per-row Refresh/Disconnect), and
pass `key_label` through `hermesRefresh`/`hermesDisconnect`. Verify per the
project's UI rule at 375px and desktop — the account list must reflow.

### 436. `request_device_code()` is still a blocking sync httpx call on the event loop

**Severity:** 🟠 High · **Status: fixed** — round 138 (`tests/test_fix_round138.py::test_request_device_code_runs_off_the_event_loop`; fixed 2026-10-14)

Wrapped in `asyncio.to_thread` like the two sibling call sites.

**Files:** `wiwi/server/app.py:6001`, `wiwi/providers/hermes_oauth.py` (`_TIMEOUT_S`,
`request_device_code`)

Round 136 threaded the two token-exchange call sites — `/poll` (`:6057`) and
`/refresh` (`:6186`) — but not the third. `request_device_code()` at `:6001` is
a plain synchronous `httpx` call executed directly in the async handler, with
the module's 30 s `_TIMEOUT_S`. It blocks the entire event loop for the
duration of the Nous round-trip: every in-flight completion, every open SSE
stream, and every pending 401 refresh hook stalls behind one admin's connect
click.

It is also the *first* request in the connect flow, so it is the one most likely
to be slow — it is the call that decides whether Nous will show a device code at
all.

**Fix sketch:** `await asyncio.to_thread(hermes_oauth.request_device_code)`,
matching the two sibling sites.

### 437. `/v1/realtime` reimplements the pre-flight and skips the `unpriced_model_policy == "reject"` gate

**Severity:** 🟠 High · **Status: fixed** — round 139 (`tests/test_fix_round139.py`; fixed 2026-10-14)

Fixed by **mirroring** the gate into `/v1/realtime` rather than
extracting the shared pre-flight helper the fix sketch asked for:
`authenticate()` renders its verdict as an HTTP error body, and the
WS path renders a `_ws_refuse` frame, so one function returning one
shape would have meant changing a surface outside this fix's file
region. **This is a weaker guarantee than one shared function** — the
two copies can still drift, and only the tests keep them honest.
`test_the_unpriced_gate_reads_identically_on_both_surfaces` runs the
same key/model/policy through `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/realtime`
and asserts identical 503s, and
`test_an_uncapped_key_is_not_refused_by_the_unpriced_gate` pins the
`max_budget is not None` narrowing, so a one-sided edit fails the
suite rather than silently diverging. A future agent who can edit
`authenticate()` should still prefer collapsing the two.

**Files:** `wiwi/server/app.py:2905-2921` (the WS admission block),
`wiwi/server/app.py:1524-1534` (the shared gate inside
`authenticate_and_authorize`), `wiwi/server/app.py:2042` / `:2351` / `:2554`
(the only `enforce_rate_limit` / `_record_tpm_usage` call sites)

The AUDIT #323 503 gate — refusing an unpriced model for a budget-capped key —
exists only inside the shared `authenticate_and_authorize` closure. `/v1/realtime`
never calls that closure: it invokes `state.auth.authenticate(token)` directly
(`:2906`) and re-implements three of the checks inline — disabled/expires
(`:2907-2912`), `over_budget` (`:2913`) and the per-key model allowlist
(`:2917-2921`) — omitting the unpriced-model gate entirely.

So the same key and the same model are refused on `/v1/chat/completions` and
admitted over the WebSocket. `enforce_rate_limit`'s only call site is `:2042`
and `_record_tpm_usage`'s are `:2351`/`:2554`, none of which the realtime path
reaches. With `unpriced_model_policy: reject` and a capped key, an unpriced
model is served over WS at a `CostEngine` price of $0, the cap never trips, and
the operator's `max_budget` silently stops applying to their most expensive
traffic class.

**Fix sketch:** extract the pre-flight into one helper both surfaces call, so
adding a check cannot silently skip one entry point (the repo forbids a second
convention beside an existing one).

### 438. The over-cap spend true-up is still under a bare `contextlib.suppress`

**Severity:** 🟠 High · **Status: fixed** — round 140 (`tests/test_fix_round140.py`; fixed 2026-10-14)

The over-cap true-up now uses the counted sibling's `try`/`except`
(logging `spend_charge_unrecorded` and incrementing
`spend_charge_failures`), and the reservation release is counted too.

**Files:** `wiwi/server/app.py:1628-1630`, `wiwi/server/app.py:1609-1626` (the
counted sibling), commit `8ee5676`

Commit `8ee5676` fixed the realtime copy of this exact pattern and left this
one, so the same method now contains two spend-recording sites with **opposite**
error handling. The sibling at `:1609-1626` wraps its `apply_spend_trueup` in a
`try/except` that logs `spend_charge_unrecorded` and increments
`spend_charge_failures`; the site at `:1628-1630` is the bare
`with contextlib.suppress(Exception):` — verbatim the second half of AUDIT #179.

This is the over-budget *crossing* path (the `if not recorded:` branch), which
is where `update_spend` returned `False` because the key went over its cap and
the charge must still be added. If that true-up raises, the exception is
swallowed: the charge is lost with no log line, and `spend_charge_failures`
stays at 0 so nothing surfaces the drift. `spend_to_date` then sits below
`max_budget` even though real money was spent, and `over_budget` may never trip
for the key that is actually over. The reservation release a few lines above
(`:1605-1607`) is uncounted in the same way.

**Fix sketch:** `try/except` matching `:1621-1626`, and count the reservation
release too.

### 439. A realtime session with no usage peak is charged $0 *and* leaves no request-log row

**Severity:** 🟠 High · **Status: fixed** — round 139 (`tests/test_fix_round139.py`; fixed 2026-10-14)

Every session that clears admission writes a request-log row and
settles tokens regardless of usage, and a no-usage session increments
the new `wiwi_realtime_usage_missing_total` counter
(`wiwi/server/metrics.py`) so the case is measurable rather than
invisible.

**Files:** `wiwi/server/app.py:515-516` (the early return),
`wiwi/server/app.py:525` (`dep.settle_tokens`), `wiwi/server/app.py:550`
(`state.logs.log_request`), `wiwi/server/app.py:2991-2992` (the `if usage is
not None` call site), `wiwi/server/app.py:501` (`_realtime_relay` returning
`None`)

`_bill_realtime_session` returns at `:515-516` — before `dep.settle_tokens`
(`:525`) and before `state.logs.log_request(...)` at `:550` — whenever the
session produced no usable usage. The call site compounds it: `if usage is not
None:` (`:2991-2992`) means a `_realtime_relay` that returns `None` (`:501`,
the handshake-failure path) never enters the billing function at all.

The realistic triggers are all ordinary failures: handshake failure or timeout
(`open_timeout=10.0`), an upstream 401 or 5xx (`:2982-2985`), or
`max_session_s` expiring before any usage-bearing frame arrives. In each case
the session is billed nothing, settles no tokens, and — most importantly —
**writes no row**, so the console shows no trace that a session happened at all
while upstream capacity was consumed. Every HTTP surface logs unconditionally
(`:2396`, `:2404`, `:2416`, `:2553`), which is what makes request-log
completeness a usable invariant; realtime is the one surface that breaks it.

**Fix sketch:** log every session that got past admission regardless of usage,
and add a `realtime_usage_missing` counter so the no-usage case is measurable
rather than invisible.

### 440. A binary frame from upstream terminates the realtime relay

**Severity:** 🟠 High · **Status: fixed** — round 139 (`tests/test_fix_round139.py`; fixed 2026-10-14)

The upstream→client loop branches on `isinstance(frame, (bytes,
bytearray, memoryview))` and forwards with `send_bytes`, so one
binary frame no longer kills the relay. The teardown log level was
also raised so a relay death is not silent.

**Files:** `wiwi/server/app.py:481` (`if '"usage"' in frame`),
`wiwi/server/app.py:486` (`await client_ws.send_text(frame)`),
`wiwi/server/app.py:487-490` (the swallow and the `finally` close),
`wiwi/server/app.py:2973` (`websockets.connect`), `wiwi/server/app.py:464`
(`iter_text`, the correct client→upstream direction)

`websockets.connect` at `:2973` is called without `decode=True`, so `recv()`
yields `str | bytes`. The upstream→client loop at `:481`/`:486` assumes `str`
unconditionally: `'"usage"' in frame` raises `TypeError` on a `bytes` operand,
and `send_text(frame)` raises on one too. That `TypeError` is caught by the bare
`except Exception` at `:487`, logged at `debug` — invisible at default verbosity
— and the `finally` at `:489-490` then closes the client socket. One binary
frame ends the whole session with no client-visible error.

The client→upstream direction is already correct: `:464` uses `iter_text()`,
which decodes. So the relay is asymmetric, and only the direction that can
actually receive binary from a misbehaving or differently-configured upstream is
the broken one.

**Fix sketch:** branch on `isinstance(frame, (bytes, bytearray))` →
`await client_ws.send_bytes(frame)`, else `send_text`; and raise the teardown log
level so a relay death is not silent.

### 441. Per-account Hermes state is never pruned — unbounded growth across reconnects

**Severity:** 🟡 Medium · **Status: fixed** — round 138 (`tests/test_fix_round138.py`; fixed 2026-10-14)

`HermesAutoRefresh.forget(provider, label)` pops the lock, the
generation counter and the breaker's streak/until/dead entries, and
`/disconnect` calls it. The generation counter is what makes it safe
against an in-flight rotation — a popped entry is treated as
"someone else owns this now", not as a restart at zero.

**Files:** `wiwi/providers/hermes_auto_refresh.py:66` (`_locks`),
`wiwi/providers/hermes_auto_refresh.py:70` (`_generations`),
`wiwi/core/recovery.py:67-69` (`CircuitBreaker._streaks` / `_until` / `_dead`)

Round 136 moved the sweeper's per-account bookkeeping onto
`(provider, key_label)` tuples, and all three structures only ever grow:
`_locks` and `_generations` get an entry on first touch of an account, and the
breaker's `_streaks`/`_until`/`_dead` dicts get one per identity it has ever
seen. Nothing pops an entry when `/disconnect` removes a key.

Compounded by #430 and #434: because every connect mints a new label (and today
stores a credential blob as it), the identity space grows without bound over a
deployment's lifetime — a long-lived gateway that has been reconnected
occidentally many times accumulates dead locks, dead generations and dead circuit
state that is never reclaimed.

**Fix sketch:** a `forget(provider, label)` that pops all three and clears the
breaker entry, called from `/disconnect`; the existing generation counter
(`hermes_auto_refresh.py:246`) already gives the race-safety needed to make it
safe against an in-flight refresh.

### 442. Round 137 left the whole-gateway backup export behind — `GET /admin/backup` silently drops `error_message`

**Severity:** 🟡 Medium · **Status: fixed** — round 141 (`tests/test_fix_round141.py`; fixed 2026-10-14)

`"error_message"` added to `_REQUEST_LOG_COLUMNS`, plus the drift
guard `test_request_log_columns_cover_every_written_column`, which
asserts every `db_sink._COLS` entry appears in
`_REQUEST_LOG_COLUMNS` ∪ `BODY_COLUMNS` so the two lists cannot
silently diverge again.

**Files:** `wiwi/server/backup.py:573-580` (`_REQUEST_LOG_COLUMNS`),
`wiwi/server/backup.py:508-521` (`_read_logs`), `wiwi/logging_core/db_sink.py:369-377`
(`_COLS`, the writer-side list that *did* gain the column)

`_REQUEST_LOG_COLUMNS` is an explicit allowlist, and round 137 added
`"error_message"` to the writer-side `_COLS` (`db_sink.py:369-377`) but not here.
`_read_logs` filters the query down to the allowlist (`:517`), so
`GET /admin/backup` omits the column with no error, no warning and no
truncation flag — an operator who exports a backup to preserve a failure's cause
(the entire point of #428) gets request logs with `error_code` and no message.

This is the **second** silent drift between the two lists; nothing asserts they
agree, so the same class of bug will recur on the next column addition.

**Fix sketch:** add `"error_message"` to `_REQUEST_LOG_COLUMNS`, and add a drift
guard test asserting every `db_sink._COLS` entry appears in
`_REQUEST_LOG_COLUMNS` ∪ `BODY_COLUMNS`.
